zmax: a Helix fork with 12 scripting languages compiled in
description:
zmax forks Helix into a zero-configuration terminal IDE: LSP, a debugger, tree-sitter, PTY terminal, magit-style git, a hex editor, a 3-pane merge resolver, and nine keymap presets (spacemacs by default, plus vim, emacs, kakoune, micro, nano, cua and others), working on first launch with no plugin manager and no setup. MPL-2.0 like upstream; provenance is in ATTRIBUTION.md.

The part that isn’t just “Helix with more.” Twelve scripting interpreters are compiled into the binary as pure-Rust crates sharing one host API, with no FFI between them: elisp, vimscript, awk, zsh, ruby, php, python, node, tcl, R, and two of my own. They’re evaluated against the live buffer, and ~/.zmax/init.el and init.vim are sourced at startup.

That buys something beyond scripting. :xpipe filters a selection through a chain of them inside the process:

:xpipe awk '{print $2}' |> php 'echo strtoupper($stdin);' |> ruby 'stdin.reverse'

No fork, no execve, no pipe file descriptors — an N-stage chain is N function calls into interpreters already linked in, and the whole chain lands as one undo step. Stages are separated by |> because a bare | is live syntax in most of the twelve. The same trick drives the fuzzy picker: the fzf.vim commands (:Files, :Rg, :GFiles) run a finder in-process rather than exec’ing fzf, while still honoring $FZF_DEFAULT_OPTS, the user’s existing config, and the FZF_* variables preview commands read. The source command behind a picker is of course still a process; the picker isn’t.

Plugins. Helix ships no plugin system. zmax hosts native compiled Rust plugins — an ordinary cdylib loaded at runtime over a frozen versioned C ABI, registering typable :-commands and reading or editing the buffer through the host API. There’s a package manager over it: :zmax-native add owner/repo clones, builds, installs and loads; installs land in a content-addressed store SHA-256 pinned in installed.toml, and loading is by mmap so the library is paged in rather than copied.

On measurement, since “IDE parity” is the kind of claim that’s usually hand-waved. Coverage is tracked against the feature surface of Vim/Neovim, Emacs, Spacemacs, kakoune, vis, sam, ed, nvi, vile, mg, nano, micro, mcedit, ne, dte, three Neovim distributions, and JetBrains. Every inventory item is parsed from that tool’s own primary source — the Neovim runtime docs, the GNU Emacs manual indexes, kakoune’s doc/pages, vile’s cmdtbl, nano’s src/global.c, ne’s texinfo — never hand-written, so the denominator isn’t something I chose. The numerator is re-derived from zmax source on every run, and a mapping that points at non-existent code is flagged broken rather than counted. Numbers live in the generated report, not the README, specifically so they can’t go stale.

The obvious objection: this is a kitchen sink, and the binary carries twelve interpreters whether you use them or not. That’s deliberate — the thesis is that zero-config means everything ships in the box — but --no-default-features drops every interpreter crate from the dependency graph if you want a lean build.

brew install MenkeTechnologies/menketech/zmax, then zmax -g fetch && zmax -g build for grammars.

title: ztmux the pure Rust tmux superset
description:
ztmux is a from-source port of tmux to Rust — the server, the client, the grid and screen model, the input parser, layouts, the command language, formats, and the terminal backend. Not a wrapper around the tmux binary and not control mode; it opens its own socket namespace (ztmux-<uid>) so it never collides with a running tmux.

Things the port doesn’t have, added beside it: triggers runs any ztmux command when a regex matches a pane’s output, which revives tmux’s removed monitor-content as a general sense-and-act loop. stack ports zellij’s StackedPanes model and realises it through tmux’s own layout engine, since tmux has no PaneGeom. pick gives you a multi-pane mark set where tmux has exactly one marked pane and all-or-nothing synchronize-panes. There’s an opt-in ratatui layer (ZTMUX_RATATUI=1) for a which-key bar and a command palette. The destructive ones — prune, bcast, equalize, layout — are dry-run by default and need -f.

cargo install ztmux. Happy to get into the gate, the parity harness, or what breaks when you move a 30-year-old C event loop into Rust.

title: zshrs, a pure rust zsh superset UNIX shell with a JIT
description:
I’ve been building zshrs, a drop-in zsh replacement that compiles shell code to bytecode and runs it on a custom VM with a Cranelift JIT.

The obvious objection is that shell performance is dominated by exec, so why JIT it. That’s true for ls | grep foo, and zshrs won’t help you there. It matters for the code that isn’t spawning processes: parameter expansion, arithmetic, pattern matching, the loops in large completion systems, and the thousand-line prompt frameworks people actually run on every keystroke. Those are interpreted tree-walks in zsh and bytecode here.

The bigger change is that a worker thread pool replaces fork/exec for builtins and function calls. This is where the semantics get interesting, and where I expect the most skepticism — $$, subshell isolation, signal disposition, and anything that depends on copy-on-write memory all need explicit handling rather than falling out of the kernel for free. I’d rather talk about the cases where this is still wrong than claim it isn’t.

On compatibility: there’s a parity test suite that runs the same inputs against 8 Bourne-family dialects and diffs behavior. “Drop-in” means my own config and plugins work, not that I’ve cleared the whole of zsh’s surface area. If you try it and your setup breaks, that’s the bug report I want.

Two things that aren’t in zsh at all:

AOP command interception — hooks around command dispatch, which turns out to be a clean place to put instrumentation that would otherwise be a wrapper function. A value-lineage provenance engine — tracking where a value in the shell came from, across expansions and command substitutions. This started as a debugging aid and became the feature I use most.

Available on crates.io and Homebrew.

Uji - Gentoo of Coding Agents
description:
My friend and I are Neovim nerds, and every so often our Neovim setups would throw errors. What did we do? We talked to each other and solved it. It was never Neovim’s fault.

We think the same way about harnesses. If you don’t like something, you shouldn’t have to call a trillion-dollar company; you should be able to fix it yourself. If you want something custom, you shouldn’t have to keep spamming some discussion thread; you should be able to write it yourself.

And more than anything, it should be simple and fast, and your computer shouldn’t scream OOM. That’s the inspiration behind uji.

I hope you all love it!!!

Shared password manager for families?
description:
Long story short, I need to have a bunch of shared accounts with family for finance and insurance and stuff, mostly for the sake of family members who are getting old and need help keeping things organized. So the requirements are:

  • Shared over long distances; just having each of us have our own password manager won't work well
  • Usable for non-techie people, so no command line stuff
  • I can self-host a web thing if necessary
  • Works on Linux and MacOS/iOS

I would just use 1Password, but recent events have demonstrated them as not exactly competent. I could always use KeepassXC and keep the file in a Google Drive folder, or maybe teach my siblings to use Syncthing, but that feels like extra steps we could do without. Anyone have any recommendations for how to do this well?
